answer: A natural place that took my breath away was Lawachara National Park, a hilly, forested area near Sreemangal in the north-east of the country. I went there with my family about two years ago, during a short winter holiday, hoping to escape our usual routine for a few days. The moment we arrived, I was struck by how [[lush]] and green everything was, with rolling tea gardens stretching across the hills on the way in. Walking through the forest, surrounded by tall trees and birdsong, was a genuinely [[humbling]] experience. At one point our guide pointed out a family of gibbons high up in the branches, and we all stood completely still, hardly daring to breathe. The air was wonderfully clean, and the whole landscape felt [[untouched]] by the chaos of modern life. We spent our days hiking along the forest trails and simply admiring the views, which were spectacular. We even crossed the railway line that runs straight through the forest, which felt like a scene from an old film. What struck me most was the profound sense of peace; being in such [[pristine]] nature made all my worries seem trivial. My grandfather, who could not join us, made me describe every detail on our next visit to the village. Honestly, I came away with a renewed appreciation for the natural world and a determination to protect it. It reminded me how important it is to [[disconnect]] and reconnect with nature.

followUps.q: Do you often visit natural places like this?
followUps.answer: Not as often as I would like. Work keeps me busy, so I usually manage one proper trip a year. In between, walking by the Jamuna is my way of staying connected to nature.

followUps.q: What could be done to protect places like this?
followUps.answer: I think visitor numbers should be controlled, and people should be taught not to leave litter or make noise. Local communities should also benefit from tourism, so they have a reason to protect the forest.

note: Named the real place (Lawachara National Park, Sreemangal) with gibbons and the railway through the forest; grandfather in the village; added mark 'disconnect'.
